scenes.heading: Building a contract that protects your design work

sents.d: Building a contract that protects your design work
A short, clear contract prevents the most common client disputes.

At minimum, a design contract should define exactly what's being delivered, how many revision rounds are included, payment terms and timing, and who owns the final files and at what point ownership transfers.

A common dispute arises when a client assumes unlimited revisions are included — stating a specific number (e.g. two rounds) in writing, with additional rounds billed separately, prevents this from becoming a point of tension later.

Requiring a deposit before starting work, and final payment before delivering final files, protects against being left unpaid after the work is done — a widely used norm in design work, not an unusual request.

take: Define deliverables, revisions and payment before you start.
